summary: Describes a BGP extension for building a confederation of autonomous systems that looks like one single autonomous system to outside peers. It was experimental and was replaced by RFC 3065.

plainLanguage.summary: A big group splits into smaller teams inside, but outsiders see just one team. This is a way to organize a huge network.

questions: how to scale ibgp with confederations
subtitle: Splitting a large autonomous system into smaller internal domains while appearing as one to the outside world.

tldr.problem: Large autonomous systems with many BGP speakers must maintain a full mesh of TCP connections for exchanging routing information, creating significant overhead and complexity. Subdividing into smaller AS domains reduces connections but complicates routing policy and exposes internal structure to the Internet.
tldr.mechanism: A confederation represents a group of member autonomous systems under a single confederation identifier. Internally, routers use their own AS numbers; externally, they advertise the confederation ID. New AS_PATH segment types (AS_CONFED_SET and AS_CONFED_SEQUENCE) hide internal topology from outside peers while allowing simple path policy control internally.
tldr.outcome: The mechanism allows large networks to simplify their internal routing architecture without exposing internal AS structure to external peers or degrading routing decisions. RFC 1965 is experimental and was superseded by RFC 3065.

facts.label: Deployment
facts.value: Already widely deployed at the time of publication

today: RFC 1965 is experimental and has been superseded by RFC 3065, which provides a revised specification for BGP confederations. However, the mechanism described in RFC 1965 remains widely used in large networks that need to scale BGP deployments.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
BGP is the protocol routers use to exchange routing information between autonomous systems. Large autonomous systems often have hundreds of BGP speakers that must all stay synchronized about available routes. Current BGP requires a full mesh: every speaker must have a TCP connection to every other speaker in the same AS. For a network with n speakers, this means each router must maintain n-1 connections, and the total number of connections grows as a quadratic function.

Subdividing a large AS into smaller internal domains could reduce this connection overhead significantly. However, simply splitting an AS exposes the internal topology to external peers, complicates policy routing based on the AS path, and can lengthen the sequence of AS numbers in routing advertisements, which some implementations use as a distance metric.

The solution is to regard a collection of AS domains under common administration as a confederation: a unified entity from the perspective of the outside world, but with internal structure optimized for the network operator's needs.
sections.plainLanguage: When many teams need to coordinate, it is expensive to have everyone talk directly to everyone else. Instead, you organize into groups where each group talks internally, and the groups talk to each other. The outside sees just one unified team.

sections.title: Confederation Terminology and Design
sections.content:
A confederation is a collection of autonomous systems advertised as a single AS number to external BGP peers. This external number is the confederation identifier. Each internal domain is a member AS and retains its own internal AS number used for routing within the confederation.

The mechanism is based on IDRP (Inter-Domain Routing Protocol), which already had the concept of routing domain confederations. Unlike IDRP, BGP confederations must be strictly hierarchical in structure due to the way BGP builds and processes the AS_PATH attribute.

RFC 1965 introduces two new types in the AS_PATH attribute: AS_CONFED_SET (an unordered set of member ASs) and AS_CONFED_SEQUENCE (an ordered set of member ASs). These mark which AS numbers are internal confederation members and which are external peers.
sections.plainLanguage: A confederation has an official ID (what outsiders see) and each internal team has its own ID (what teams inside use). Special labels on messages say whether an AS number is internal or external to the confederation.

sections.title: Operation Inside and Outside
sections.content:
When a confederation member router talks to another member in the same confederation, it uses its own member AS number. When it talks to an external peer outside the confederation, it uses the confederation identifier. The router receiving an AS_PATH attribute that contains its own confederation ID treats the path the same way it would treat its own AS number—as a loop indicator.

The RFC replaces BGP's AS_PATH modification rules with a new set. When advertising a route within the confederation (to another member AS), the router simply prepends its own member AS number to a confed-type segment. When advertising to an external peer, the router removes all confederation-type path segments and advertises only the confederation identifier, preventing the outside world from seeing how the internal structure is organized.
sections.plainLanguage: Inside the group, teams use their real team numbers when passing messages. Outside the group, they use the group number. The routing system throws away the internal team numbers before messages leave the group.

sections.title: Implementation and Compatibility
sections.content:
All BGP speakers within a confederation must support the new confederation segment types. A router that does not recognize AS_CONFED_SET or AS_CONFED_SEQUENCE will reject the message and send an "UPDATE Message Error" notification. This means confederation support must be deployed consistently within a confederation, but external peers do not need to support it at all.

At the time RFC 1965 was written, the authors noted that the mechanism was already widely deployed. This broad deployment meant the choice to extend the existing AS_PATH attribute rather than using a separate optional attribute could not be changed without breaking deployed systems.

The RFC permits member ASs to share common administration and internal IGP information. The restriction on advertising certain attributes like LOCAL_PREFERENCE to neighboring ASs is lifted for confederation members, allowing them to use the same path selection criteria as same-AS speakers.
sections.plainLanguage: All the teams inside the group must speak the same language about internal messages. Teams outside the group do not need to understand that language, so they can be left out of the upgrade.

sections.title: Security and Deployment Notes
sections.content:
The RFC explicitly states that security issues are not discussed in the document. The mechanism is purely an organizational tool; it does not provide encryption, authentication, or protection against forged routing advertisements. Like all BGP deployments, confederations should be protected by other means such as MD5-based BGP session authentication.

The confederation concept does obscure internal topology from the outside world, which provides a small degree of operational security by hiding the number and structure of internal domains from external observers. However, this is a side effect, not a security feature.
sections.plainLanguage: The confederation mechanism does not add any locks or security. Network operators must protect the routing system the same way they do for regular BGP.
